1:
The name and the author are settled at the door. Keil and Delitzsch note that in the Hebrew manuscripts the collection is headed by the word that opens three of the five pieces, the cry alas, how, while the Rabbis name it from its contents, the Greek and Latin titles following them. Clarke adds that in the Chaldee it has no name at all and that anciently it was written consecutively with the last chapter of the prophecy. On the author he finds no contest, since the whole current of antiquity and of modern times points to Jeremiah and the style is sufficient evidence; but he records one dissent, from a learned man who supposed the five chapters were written by Daniel and his three companions and by Jeconiah, and remarks that none has ever been converted to that opinion. On the occasion there has been more difference: some think it composed on the death of Josiah, others on the destruction of the city, to which all its parts seem best to apply.

Ellicott describes the shape. The poem divides into two symmetrical halves, the prophet lamenting over the city in the first and the daughter of Zion bewailing her own miseries in the second; each verse has three lines, and in the Hebrew each begins with the same letter. He would join the clauses into one sentence, she is become a widow that was great among the nations, and holds that tributary implies personal servitude rather than the money payment for which it was afterwards commuted.

Calvin explains the astonishment. The Prophet assumes the person of one filled with amazement at something new and unexpected, and the thing was incredible, since the city was chosen for God to dwell in and might have been thought exempt from all danger. Its state was founded by a celestial decree, and the promise that here is my rest for ever seemed to raise it above the clouds. When it fell, the Temple burnt and the king driven into exile, this thought especially must have upset the faith of all: what does God mean, and how is it that he promised this city would be perpetual?

Henry walks through the losses. She was full of her own people and of others who resorted to her for commerce and for converse, and now her own are carried into captivity and strangers make no court to her. The chief places are no longer places of concourse where wisdom cried, and justly are they left unfrequented, since the cry of wisdom there was not heard; those ever so much increased, he adds, God can soon diminish. Let no state, he adds, not this city nor Babylon herself, say, I sit as a queen and shall never sit as a widow. Wesley says it in a line, that she who had a God for a husband is now forsaken of him and stripped of her king.

The weeping is measured. Keil and Delitzsch hold that the doubled verb expresses not the continuance of the action but its intensity, so that she weeps bitterly, and that night is named as the time when grief gives place to sleep, so that tears which do not cease even then argue an overwhelming sorrow. Calvin takes the doubling the other way, of a weeping without intermission, since night is given us for rest; and he corrects a rendering, that the word means not jaws but cheeks, since tears may be restrained, but when they cover the whole face it is evidence of great mourning. Gill reports the Jewish reading of the doubled verb as two weepings, one for each temple, and notes from Jarchi that the temple was burnt in the night. Ellicott identifies the lovers and friends as the nations the kingdom had allied with, Egypt and the Edomites and Moabites among them, which afterwards turned against her.
3:
The first line divides them over what kind of going is meant. Calvin says interpreters apply it improperly to the captivity: before the Prophet bewails the exile he says Judah had been scattered, since many who fled the cruelty of enemies went into voluntary exile, some concealing themselves with the Moabites and many going into Egypt, so that there was no country in which some of the Jews were not fugitives. He diagnoses the error too: those who take exile to be meant must make the servitude the cruelty the people had exercised on their own servants, whereas it would be absurd to say they migrated on account of affliction and migrated willingly, when they were driven by the Chaldeans. Ellicott sets the alternative: the received version suggests a voluntary emigration of those who went to Egypt to avoid oppression at home, but the Hebrew admits the rendering from affliction, and then the words speak of a forcible deportation to a worse misery abroad. Wesley takes the servitude at home, of oppression by their rulers and of masters keeping servants beyond the jubilee; the pursuers, he adds, overtook them where they could not escape.

On the last clause Clarke asks whether the words refer to the attempt of Zedekiah and the princes to get out of the city by the gates between the two walls, from which no escape was possible.

The mourning ways are a figure, and must then be located. Keil and Delitzsch, who report that reading of the first verse as the common modern one, refuse two identifications here: the ways are not the streets of the city, which have a different name, nor the highways leading out of Zion; they are the roads leading up to the city, and they mourn, that is, are deserted, because no one goes up any longer to observe the feasts, for which same reason the gates are in ruins. They add why priests and virgins are conjoined, that the lament is over the cessation of the feasts, and Ellicott says the virgins are named as taking part in the hymns and processions of the festivals. Gill draws it out: ways may be said to rejoice when many pass along them and to mourn when none is seen, and the roads on which companies travelled up three times a year now carry no one and are overgrown with grass. Clarke calls it a fine prosopopoeia and observes that all poets of eminence among the Greeks and Romans use the image, citing the lament of Moschus for Bion and of Virgil for Daphnis, where woods and rivers are made to weep.

Calvin agrees that feelings belong not to ways, and thinks the figure more emphatic than if the people had been shown mourning. What it registers is the heaviest loss of all: when the Jews saw that the worship of God had fallen it was more grievous than to be bereaved of children or plundered of their goods, since in that worship consisted the salvation of their souls. He guards the point at once. The worship of God was not tied to ceremonies, for Daniel never ceased to pray and was heard in exile no less than if he had made an offering in the Temple; but God had not instituted these rites in vain, and the Prophet exhibits the thing by its symbols.

The last verse turns the law back on them. Keil and Delitzsch note that the adversaries have become the head and Judah the tail, as was threatened in the address of Moses, where the reverse had been intended; and the enemies, knowing their power supreme, are quite at ease and secure. The children of tender age are driven off like a flock, the comparison to lambs carried by the preposition; Gill says the Chaldeans had the dominion and obliged the people to be subject.
6:
Calvin lists what the departed beauty was: God had chosen there a habitation, a sacerdotal kingdom was there, the people were his heritage, and there he had deposited his covenant, so that Moses could ask what nation was so illustrious. Gill puts the losses in a line: the kingdom removed, the priesthood ceased, the temple burnt. On the harts he observes that they are swift by nature and, when pressed by want, run as though flying, so that princes who had walked with gravity and the appearance of authority were now swift like harts oppressed with hunger. Ellicott gives the figure a date, referring it to the flight and capture of Zedekiah, who with his sons and princes fell into enemy hands like fainting and stricken deer.

What is remembered is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch will not let the days of affliction be a second object of the verb: the object is all her pleasant things, and if the days were intended too a copula would be required, which one expositor supplies arbitrarily. Calvin canvasses the word rendered miseries: some derive it from a root meaning to complain or to migrate and render exile, others from a root meaning to fail and render want; he does not approve of complaint, and thinks exile or want the best. He also draws the moral, that while the city flourished she did not consider the blessings of God, ingratitude being an abyss which absorbs all his fullness.

The mocking at her sabbaths raises two questions. Clarke reports that some contend sabbaths are not intended at all, since the Greek gives her habitation, the Chaldee her good things and the Syriac her breach, while the Latin and Arabic agree with the Hebrew; his oldest manuscripts and many of Kennicott have the word in the plural. He then supplies the mockery: the Jews were despised for keeping the sabbath, and Juvenal says every seventh day was a blank to them. Clarke answers that the Roman calendar gave many more idle days than God had prescribed, and that the sabbath is a most wise and beneficent ordinance. Ellicott takes the word as coined: found nowhere else, though connected with the ordinary word for sabbath, it seems made to express at once the enforced sabbaths of the untilled land and the sabbaths which, after the Temple was destroyed, were no longer festivals but empty of any religious rite.

Then the cause. Gill notes that the Hebrew has, she hath sinned a sin, a great sin as the Targum takes it, which some make idolatry and others covenant breaking, though perhaps no one sin is meant. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the derivation the ancient expositors gave the next word and make it a lengthened form of the term for uncleanness, transferred to Jerusalem, personified as such a woman and therefore shunned. Ellicott says the same of the verb, used technically of the separation of a woman under ceremonial defilement, and adds that the figure is continued with startling boldness, since she would fain turn her back on those who exult in the twofold nakedness of her sin and its punishment.

Calvin closes by contrasting this lament with another kind. The Prophet did not compose his song as the heathen did, and Calvin sets beside it the lament in Virgil over the fall of Troy, where the speaker cries that Ilium has been, and that a cruel Jupiter has transferred all things to Argos. That complaint accuses God of cruelty, and is put in the mouth of a priest of Apollo. We hence see, he says, how the unbelieving, lamenting their calamities, vomit forth blasphemies against God, exasperated by sorrow. Very different is the Prophet, who while deploring the miseries of his people adds that God is a righteous avenger, and reminds them to humble themselves and confess that they justly deserved their evils.
9:
The figure is carried further, and Calvin breaks with the others over what it means. Gill takes the filthiness for sin made manifest, the allusion being to a woman whose uncleanness flows down to her skirts and is there seen; Ellicott says the picture is pushed to its most loathsome extreme; Keil and Delitzsch define the word as the defilement caused by touching a person or thing Levitically unclean, here defilement by sins, revealed at last by the judgment. Calvin holds that interpreters are mistaken, and that the reference is not to guilt but to punishment. The Prophet alludes to those who hide their uncleanness as much as they can, but such hiding is of no avail, since nature must have its course; shame often makes men conceal their evils and bear them silently, but this people could not hide their disgrace.

On the forgotten end they agree. Keil and Delitzsch point to the warning in the song of Moses, that if they were wise they would think of their end, and add that the words are a quotation from Isaiah, where they are used of Babylon, which thought she would always remain mistress and did not think of the end of her pride, so that on her too came the sentence to come down from her glory and sit in the dust. Clarke, with Blayney, says that though evident marks of her pollution appeared about her, she had no thought of the consequence at the last. Ellicott would render the verb as past, she remembered not, and makes her recklessness about the future what brought her down so far. He also assigns the prayer that closes the verse: the words are not the prophet but Zion, anticipating the personation which begins systematically further on.

What the pleasant things were is disputed. Gill takes them for the precious things in the house of God, the ark, the table, the altar and the vessels of the sanctuary, and reports that Jarchi makes the enemy the Moabites and Ammonites, who seized the books of the law and burnt them because there was a law in them forbidding their entrance into the congregation, though the Targum better explains it of the Chaldeans. Ellicott says a like phrase is used elsewhere of the vessels of the Temple, which leads us to think primarily of them, though the word includes all works of art and ornament. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the restriction, since neither the sense of the word nor the structure of the clauses limits the pleasant things to the treasures of the sanctuary. Calvin takes them for the invaluable treasures God had deposited with the chosen people rather than anything of an earthly and fading life, and Wesley says the things of the sanctuary were always pleasant to those that feared God.

The profanation weighs heavier than the plunder. Ellicott notes that the stress falls there, since the Ammonites and Moabites were excluded from the congregation and yet now rushed with other heathen even into the holy of holies, which none but the high priest might enter. Calvin says it was more grievous to the faithful to see the Temple polluted than to lose their property and wander in exile; the sanctuary is called the sanctuary of the people, since God had not caused it to be built for his own benefit but for theirs; and the enemy entered not to worship but by force, to violate it and abolish the worship of God. Then the famine. Keil and Delitzsch note that the participles express a permanent condition and refuse to restrict the want to the siege, since even after the city was reduced the shortage may have continued, its starved inhabitants delivering their most valuable things to the very men who had plundered them, for food. Gill observes that it is not the priests only who sigh but all the people.
12:
The two words that open the verse are hard, and every voice reports the options. Keil and Delitzsch note that the Latin gives O all ye and the Chaldee I adjure you all, the old versions taking the word as an exclamation; they resist repointing it, since a verb would then have to be supplied, and reject the proposal that the prophet means, not to you, passers-by, do I cry this, since passers-by could hardly regard a call addressed to God as applying to them. Calvin lists the same possibilities: some read it as a question, others more simply, I see that I am not cared for by you, others as a prayer of goodwill, let not such sorrow be upon you; he prefers the question, the note of interrogation being often omitted. Ellicott renders it literally, not to you, ye passers by, and judges the received version best, since what the mourning city felt most keenly was that her unparalleled sufferings were met with an unparalleled indifference. Gill adds two more, one deprecating and one adjuring.

Calvin explains why strangers are addressed. Had she spoken to neighbours only there would not have been so much force in it; by speaking to those who merely pass along the road she shows that her calamity was so great that it ought to have roused the sympathy of men from the remotest parts, even on their journey. Clarke agrees that the desolations had scarcely any parallel, and adds that excessive abuse of accumulated mercies calls for singular and exemplary punishment.

Henry allows the claim and then turns it on the reader. This might perhaps be truly said of the griefs of Jerusalem, but we apply it too readily to ourselves when in trouble; because we feel most from our own burden we cry out that surely never was sorrow like our sorrow, whereas if all troubles were thrown into a common stock and an equal dividend made, rather than stand to that we should each of us say, pray give me my own again. He then works the figures of the next verse. She is as one in a fever, and the fever is of God sending; she is as one in a net, which the more he struggles to get out of the more he is entangled in, and the net is of God spreading, for the enemies could not have succeeded had not God spread a net for her feet.

What the bones are divides them. Gill reports the Targum as interpreting them of her fortified places, the temple and the palaces, burnt by the fire of the Chaldeans but said to be sent from above because it was by the direction of the Lord, as though struck with lightning; he allows also that the fire of divine wrath may be meant, which was like a burning fever. Calvin says those who interpret the bones of fortified places weaken the meaning, and takes the word in its proper sense, of a fire penetrating to the inmost parts, since by bones is denoted strength, as when David deplored that his bones were vexed. The phrase from above he calls emphatic, since it was no common burning, but such as betokened the dreadful power of God, as though he had thundered from heaven. Ellicott says the words are probably figurative, the judgments being a fire from heaven piercing to the joints and marrow, and Wesley calls it a judgment as consuming and afflictive as fire. On the turning back Ellicott is careful: the phrase points not to defeat and flight in battle but completes the figure of the net, painting the failure of every effort to escape, and the word for desolate implies, as in the case of Tamar, an utter and hopeless misery. Calvin says the same, that she was ensnared and bound over to ruin, as one fallen into toils.
14:
Calvin says interpreters explain the words without touching the meaning, because they do not see the continued metaphor. Two things are to be held together, that the hand of God holds the yoke tied and that the yoke is bound round the neck. As a husbandman, having tied a yoke on his oxen, holds the rein and folds it about his hand, so that they can neither throw off the yoke nor disobey him, so the yoke of these iniquities was fastened: I bear it, she says, but it is tied so that it cannot be shaken off, and however I kick, God holds it by his own hand and constrains me to bear it. The verse does two things at once, bewailing the grievousness of the calamity and confessing that God was justly incensed.

Ellicott works on the words. The verb is found nowhere else but was probably a technical term for the twisting of the thongs by which a yoke was fastened, the yoke here being the transgressions of Judah; and in the clause that follows he would read it hath made rather than he hath made, the subject being the yoke that was above her strength. He notes besides that here, and in thirteen other passages of this book, the divine name used is Adonai rather than the more usual Jehovah, as though the covenant name were less appropriate in the lips of one who lay under his condemnation. Clarke turns the image inward: I am tied and bound by the chain of my sins, so wreathed, doubled and twisted round me that I cannot free myself, which he calls a fine representation of the miseries of a penitent soul, feeling that nothing but the pitifulness of the mercy of God can loose it. Wesley reads the wreathing as a complication of judgments twisted like cords, sword and famine and captivity; Gill notes that the punishment was laid on by the Lord himself, the Chaldeans being only instruments.

The treading is rendered three ways. Ellicott would have it made contemptible, as of those weighed in the balance and found wanting, and observes that the adjective for the mighty men is used elsewhere of bulls but stands here for the heroes of Judah. Keil and Delitzsch take the verb for one meaning to lift up or tear away forcibly, and reject the sense of outweighing, which would make the warriors so many weights raised when the Chaldean power was thrown into the scale. Gill keeps the plainer picture, of men trodden as mire is trodden in the streets. Where they fell matters to both: they fell not in open battle but ignominiously in the midst of the captured city, and Calvin says that had they fallen on the field it would not have been so grievous, but to be laid prostrate in the bosom of the city was a token of vengeance from above.

The assembly divides them. Ellicott finds the point of the phrase in its being the one used for proclaiming a religious festival: here the festival is proclaimed not for the city but against her, kept by those who exult in the slaughter of her young warriors. Clarke and Wesley take it of the Chaldean army, which God commissioned to destroy the city. Calvin at first prefers another sense, the fixed time appointed by God to destroy the strong men, and thinks the rendering assembly forced; but he grants that to call a fixed time against a person is no suitable expression, and concludes that the received rendering is right. On the winepress Ellicott would render that God has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter, and Wesley that he trod upon them as men stamp grapes. Gill closes with the weeping, which he gives to the godly among them, and particularly to Jeremiah, weeping both for the sins committed and for the punishment inflicted.
17:
The spreading of the hands is a gesture, and Calvin disposes of two rivals. He takes it as a token of sorrow, or the seeking of friends, since when we wish to move men to pity we stretch forth our arms; he wonders how it came into the minds of some to say that Jerusalem had broken bread with her hands, which he calls extremely puerile, and refuses the rendering that she clapped them as a harsh mode of speaking. Ellicott calls it the attitude of eastern prayer, or of lamentation and despair; Clarke says it is the form used in supplication; Gill allows either a submitting to the conqueror or a calling to friends. Keil and Delitzsch notice something else, that here the writer breaks in on the lamentation with a contemplative digression, as if the voice of the weeping one were choked with tears, introducing a pause which divides the lamentation in two and gives a turn to its contents.

Ellicott would recast the next clause: better, that those round about him should be his adversaries, the nearest neighbours being the bitterest foes; Keil and Delitzsch say the same of the neighbouring nations, all striving to increase his misery. Calvin uses the clause to fix the blame: these evils did not come through men, and lest they ascribe their sorrow to the Chaldeans, as was commonly done, the Prophet recalls their attention to God himself, since the Chaldeans, cruel as they were, did nothing through their own impulse but by the command of God. On the last figure Clarke notes that none dared approach such a woman, to help or comfort her, because of the law; Ellicott says it might be rendered as one polluted; Wesley says she is become loathsome and filthy.

The confession that follows changes the tone. Gill observes that good men always own that God is righteous in all his ways, though they sometimes know not how to reconcile his providences with his promises and his declared love. Ellicott hears an echo of an earlier prophecy and says misery does its work and issues in repentance, the suffering coming from the all-righteous Judge; and he thinks it significant that with this beginning of conversion the name Jehovah reappears. Calvin explains the mouth of God as the prophetic doctrine, and finds the phrase emphatic: when the word of God was proclaimed by prophets it was despised as an empty sound, and so God calls whatever his servants declare his own mouth. To provoke that mouth was less excusable than simply to offend God, for the ungodly often offend while labouring under ignorance, but when the Lord opens his mouth to recall the erring and show the way of salvation, and men then rush headlong into sins, it is a mark of extreme impiety.

The last verse is disputed as to its time and its close. Keil and Delitzsch deny that it continues the address to the nations, taking it for a complaint made to God, and refuse to read the verbs as preterites: they indicate accomplished facts whose consequences reach to the present, since it was not merely during the siege that she called for help, but she calls even now, and in vain. Gill allows the lovers to be either her idols or the Egyptians who courted her friendship and left her to stand or fall alone; he notes that the Targum makes the deceivers the Romans who came with Titus and Vespasian. Clarke says simply, my allies, the Egyptians. Ellicott would read called to rather than called for, and observes that the famine is emphasised by the fact that even the priests and elders, the guides of the people, died of hunger. At the end he prefers the received text: two old versions supply by conjecture the words and found not, but there is more force in the suggestive silence of the Hebrew.
20:
Gill traces the movement of the chapter in a line: she turns from one to another, sometimes addressing strangers who pass by, sometimes calling to her lovers, and at other times to God, which is best of all. Calvin makes the turn the mark of difference between this lament and a heathen one. The faithful first acknowledge that they are justly chastised, and then trust in his mercy and implore his aid; by these two marks, repentance and faith, the Church is distinguished from the unbelieving. To sigh and mourn in adversity is common to both, but the children of God humble themselves under his mighty hand, whereas the ungodly pour forth their complaints into the air, and when nature dictates that they ought to address God, no prayer arises from a sincere heart. When we flee to him humbly, he says, we in a manner unburden our sorrows into his bosom.

The words for the inward parts are weighed. Keil and Delitzsch note that the form of the verb occurs elsewhere only twice, once of the countenance, where it can mean only to be glowing red; they are unwilling to derive it from the root for redness and refer it rather to one meaning to ferment or rise into froth. The bowels, they add, are the nobler internal organs, the seat of the affections. Ellicott says bowels and heart are almost synonyms for the deepest emotions of the soul, and that the word for troubled might be better rendered inflamed.

The last clause draws out the classical parallels. Ellicott takes the small word before death as giving the emphasis of the undefined: it is not death simply that makes each home tremble, but its many shapes, the starvation and disease and exhaustion which were all deathlike in their working, and he quotes a phrase of Virgil for it. Clarke gathers a whole set of them. Virgil, on the fall of Troy, has all parts resounding with tumults and fears, and grisly death appearing in sundry shapes; Milton has Despair tending the sick while over them triumphant Death shook his dart; Jeremiah himself has death coming up into the windows; and Silius Italicus has Death stalking along and opening his hideous throat to gulp down the people. Wesley says the death meant is by famine and pestilence.

Calvin notes a defect in the grammar of the next verse, the verb standing twice but the first time without a nominative, so the sentence hangs till the second clause supplies it. Sympathy is commonly shown towards the miserable, he says, and our evil is doubled when we become a spectacle to enemies, who derive joy from our adversities. He reports a further view without adopting it, that the enemies rejoiced the more because they were persuaded that God was displeased with his own people. Ellicott refers the words historically to the Edomites.

The day at the end is disputed. Ellicott would render it proclaimed rather than called, and reports that some take the first verb as a perfect, thou hast brought, making the day that of vengeance upon Judah; but with the received rendering the clause coheres better with what follows, and the day is that of the punishment of the foes. Clarke takes it the same way, that Babylon shall be visited in her turn and the judgments poured on her shall equal her state with the mourner, and Wesley that God had foretold their destruction and proclaimed it by the prophet. On the closing imprecation Clarke enters a caution: such imprecations in the sacred writings are generally to be understood as declarative of the evils they name, or that such evils will take place, since no prophet of God ever wished desolation on those against whom he was directed to prophesy. He adds that though the judgments of God are slow, they are sure.
